cards.q: What is the difference between raylib and a game engine?
cards.a: raylib is a library of functions you call from your own loop; an engine provides an editor, scene structure and systems that your game fits into.
cards.lessonTitle: What raylib Is and Setting It Up

cards.q: What does `vcpkg integrate install` do?
cards.a: It makes Visual Studio projects find the headers and libraries installed by vcpkg without any project settings.
cards.lessonTitle: What raylib Is and Setting It Up

cards.q: Why does `WindowShouldClose` become true?
cards.a: When the user presses Esc or clicks the window's close button.
cards.lessonTitle: What raylib Is and Setting It Up

cards.q: What are the three steps of every frame?
cards.a: Read input, update the world, draw the world.

cards.q: What happens if you do not clear the background?
cards.a: The new frame is drawn on top of an old one, so moving objects leave trails.

cards.q: Where does raylib read the keyboard and mouse?
cards.a: In `EndDrawing`, ready for the next frame.

cards.q: Which way does y grow in screen coordinates?
cards.a: Downwards: the top of the window is y = 0.

cards.q: Where is the position of a rectangle and of a circle?
cards.a: A rectangle's position is its top-left corner; a circle's is its centre.

cards.q: How do you centre text horizontally?
cards.a: Measure it with `MeasureText` and start it at (screen width - text width) / 2.

cards.q: Why multiply speeds by `GetFrameTime()`?
cards.a: So movement is measured per second and is the same at every frame rate.

cards.q: Why is diagonal movement too fast without normalising?
cards.a: The direction (1, 1) has length about 1.41, so the speed is 41 % higher.

cards.q: Why clamp dt?
cards.a: A very long frame would move objects so far that they skip through walls; clamping keeps steps small.

cards.q: When do you use IsKeyDown and when IsKeyPressed?
cards.a: Down for things that continue while held, such as moving; Pressed for one-off actions, such as jumping or choosing a menu item.

cards.q: Why read typed text with GetCharPressed instead of key codes?
cards.a: It gives real characters for the user's keyboard layout and Shift state.

cards.q: What is a dead zone?
cards.a: A small range around the stick's rest position that is treated as zero, so drift does not move the character.

cards.q: What is the difference between an Image and a Texture2D?
cards.a: An Image is pixels in main memory for editing; a Texture2D is in video memory and is what you draw.

cards.q: Why must textures be loaded after InitWindow?
cards.a: Creating a texture needs the OpenGL context that InitWindow makes.

cards.q: How do you draw a sprite facing the other way?
cards.a: Give DrawTexturePro (or DrawTextureRec) a source rectangle with a negative width.

cards.q: Why should animation time be measured in seconds, not game frames?
cards.a: So the animation plays at the same speed whatever the frame rate.

cards.q: Why must play() not restart an animation that is already playing?
cards.a: It is called every frame; restarting each time would keep the animation on its first frame.

cards.q: What is the difference between a looping and a one-shot animation?
cards.a: A looping animation wraps back to its first frame; a one-shot stops on its last frame and reports that it has finished.

cards.q: Why should you not keep the pointer TextFormat returns?
cards.a: It points to a buffer inside raylib that is reused by later calls.
cards.lessonTitle: Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface

cards.q: How do you right-align a score at x = 780?
cards.a: Measure the text and draw it at 780 - width.
cards.lessonTitle: Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface

cards.q: Why is the interface drawn outside the camera?
cards.a: So it stays fixed on the screen while the world moves under it.
cards.lessonTitle: Text, Fonts and a Simple Interface

cards.q: When do you use Sound and when Music?
cards.a: Sound for short effects loaded fully into memory; Music for long tracks streamed from the file.

cards.q: What happens if you forget UpdateMusicStream?
cards.a: The stream's buffer is not refilled, so the music stops almost straight away.

cards.q: Why use sound aliases?
cards.a: Playing a Sound that is already playing restarts it; aliases let several copies play at the same time.

cards.q: What makes a set of screens a state machine?
cards.a: There is always exactly one current screen, and events move the game from one screen to another.

cards.q: Why is a stack useful for a pause menu?
cards.a: The game stays below the menu, frozen and still drawn, and popping the menu returns to it exactly as it was.

cards.q: Why should scenes request stack changes instead of changing the stack directly?
cards.a: Popping the scene whose update is running would destroy it while its code is still executing.

cards.q: What is an AABB?
cards.a: An axis-aligned bounding box: a rectangle whose sides are parallel to the x and y axes.

cards.q: Why compare squared distances for circles?
cards.a: It gives the same answer as comparing distances, without the cost of a square root.

cards.q: How do you test a circle against a rectangle?
cards.a: Clamp the circle's centre to the rectangle to find the closest point, and check whether that point is within the radius.

cards.q: Which axis do you push an object out along?
cards.a: The one where the overlap is smaller: the shortest way out.

cards.q: Why move and resolve one axis at a time?
cards.a: The direction of each single-axis move tells you which side was hit, characters slide along walls, and they do not catch on seams between tiles.

cards.q: What is tunnelling?
cards.a: A fast object jumping completely past a thin obstacle between two frames, so no overlap is ever detected.

cards.q: How do you get gravity and jump speed from a jump height h and a rise time t?
cards.a: gravity = 2h / t², jump speed = 2h / t.

cards.q: What is coyote time?
cards.a: A short time after walking off a ledge during which the player can still jump.

cards.q: Why clear both the coyote and buffer timers when jumping?
cards.a: Otherwise the same press or the same ledge can trigger a second jump.

cards.q: What does the accumulator hold?
cards.a: Real time that has passed but has not been simulated yet, less than one step after the loop.

cards.q: What is the spiral of death, and how do you avoid it?
cards.a: Steps that take longer than real time make each frame slower than the last; limit the steps per frame or clamp the frame time.

cards.q: What is alpha in interpolation?
cards.a: accumulator / step: how far the current time is between the last two simulation steps.

cards.q: What are the broad phase and the narrow phase?
cards.a: The broad phase cheaply finds pairs that might collide; the narrow phase runs the exact test on those pairs only.

cards.q: Why is an object inserted into every cell it touches?
cards.a: So that two objects on opposite sides of a cell boundary still share a cell and are tested.

cards.q: How do you avoid testing the same pair twice?
cards.a: Only test pairs with a < b and remember pairs already tested, or test a pair only in one agreed cell.

cards.q: What do a Camera2D's target and offset mean?
cards.a: The target is the world point the camera looks at; the offset is where on the screen that point is drawn.

cards.q: How do you find which world point the mouse is over?
cards.a: GetScreenToWorld2D(GetMousePosition(), camera).

cards.q: What is a camera dead zone?
cards.a: A box around the screen's centre within which the player can move without the camera moving.

cards.q: Why store a tile map as one flat vector?
cards.a: It is a single block of memory indexed with y * width + x, which is fast and simple.

cards.q: What happens to object letters such as P or E when loading a level?
cards.a: Their positions are recorded in object lists, and the map gets an empty tile there.

cards.q: How does 4-neighbour auto-tiling choose a tile?
cards.a: It builds a 4-bit number from which neighbours are solid and uses it to pick one of 16 pictures.

cards.q: Why use a fixed pool for particles?
cards.a: It avoids allocating and freeing memory for hundreds of short-lived objects every second.

cards.q: How does "swap and pop" remove particle i?
cards.a: Copy the last living particle into slot i and reduce the living count by one.

cards.q: When do you use additive blending?
cards.a: For things that emit light, such as fire, sparks and magic, so overlaps glow brighter.

cards.q: Why should every state change go through one enter function?
cards.a: So the timer is always reset and the state's start actions always run, from wherever the change comes.

cards.q: How do you test whether the player is in an enemy's field of view?
cards.a: Compare the dot product of the facing direction and the direction to the player with the cosine of half the view angle.

cards.q: What is telegraphing?
cards.a: Showing an attack is coming, such as a wind-up animation, so the player has time to react.

cards.q: Why does BFS find a shortest path when all steps cost the same?
cards.a: It reaches tiles in order of their distance from the start, so the first time it reaches the goal is by a shortest path.

cards.q: What are g, h and f in A*?
cards.a: g is the cost so far, h is the estimated remaining cost, and f = g + h; A* expands the smallest f first.

cards.q: When is a flow field better than many path searches?
cards.a: When many units head for the same target: one search from the target serves all of them.

cards.q: Which way does y point in raylib's 3D space?
cards.a: Up.

cards.q: What is the difference between perspective and orthographic projection?
cards.a: Perspective makes distant things smaller; orthographic keeps sizes the same at every distance.

cards.q: What does the dot product of two normalised directions tell you?
cards.a: The cosine of the angle between them: 1 for the same direction, 0 for perpendicular, -1 for opposite.

cards.q: Why is the pitch clamped?
cards.a: So the camera never looks straight up or down past the vertical, where the view would flip.

cards.q: Why walk with the flat forward direction instead of the full look direction?
cards.a: So looking up or down does not change walking speed or push the player into the floor or sky.

cards.q: How does a third-person camera find its position?
cards.a: It starts from a point on the player and moves back along the view direction by the camera distance.

cards.q: How do you find what the mouse is pointing at in 3D?
cards.a: Turn the mouse position into a ray from the camera with GetScreenToWorldRay, test it against the objects and keep the nearest hit.

cards.q: In the slab method, when does the ray miss the box?
cards.a: When the latest entry into a slab comes after the earliest exit from another (tmin > tmax).

cards.q: Why keep the hit with the smallest distance?
cards.a: A ray can pass through several objects; the nearest one is the one actually seen or hit.

cards.q: What do the vertex shader and the fragment shader do?
cards.a: The vertex shader positions each vertex; the fragment shader chooses the colour of each pixel a triangle covers.

cards.q: What is a uniform?
cards.a: A value set from the program that is the same for every vertex and pixel of a draw call.

cards.q: Why does a light shader need screenHeight - y for the light position?
cards.a: gl_FragCoord measures y from the bottom of the window, while raylib's screen coordinates measure it from the top.

cards.q: Why is the source height negative when drawing a render texture?
cards.a: OpenGL stores textures upside down relative to raylib's screen coordinates, so the picture must be flipped vertically.

cards.q: How do you apply a shader to the whole frame?
cards.a: Draw the frame into a render texture, then draw that texture to the screen between BeginShaderMode and EndShaderMode.

cards.q: How do you compute a pixel's perceived brightness for grey scale?
Why start from defaults when loading settings?
cards.a: Missing, damaged or new keys then keep sensible values instead of breaking the game.

cards.q: How do you save without risking a half-written file?
cards.a: Write to a temporary file and rename it over the old one, which replaces it in one step.

cards.q: What does a checksum protect against, and what not?
cards.a: It detects damaged or cut-off files; it does not stop someone from editing the file on purpose.

cards.q: Why does a game often show a black window when started outside Visual Studio?
cards.a: The working directory is different, so relative asset paths do not find the files; ChangeDirectory(GetApplicationDirectory()) fixes it.

cards.q: Why link the runtime statically for a release?
cards.a: So players do not need the Visual C++ Redistributable or other DLLs installed.

cards.q: What changes in the main loop for a web build?
cards.a: The browser must call one frame function repeatedly, so the loop becomes emscripten_set_main_loop(frame, 0, 1).

cards.q: Why describe waves as data rather than code?
cards.a: They can be changed and rebalanced without recompiling, even while the game runs.

cards.q: Why build the game in an order where it always runs?
cards.a: You can test the feel at every step, and you always have a working game to show if you stop.

cards.q: What should be in the game before you call it complete?
cards.a: A start, a goal, an end with a score, play again, saved settings, sound, and a build others can run.
